newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Quota violators and Iraqi oil perplex OPEC.
newsitem.headline: Quota violators and Iraqi oil perplex OPEC.

text.p: Saudi Arabia is predicting a reasonably firm world oil price, despite what is likely to be another failure by OPEC this week to persuade its mavericks to stop violating mandated production limits.

Delegates forecast that a Saudi-backed majority at ministerial talks of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, opening on Wednesday, would favour the expedient of a freeze of current quotas until year's end.
These already provide, on paper, for what Iraq declared on Tuesday would be a renewal within 10 days of U.N.-supervised sales of its oil under relaxed Gulf War sanctions.

But the delegates doubted if those of the 11 OPEC members who, like Venezuela, are alleged to be exceeding their limits would do much to curb a flow of surplus oil - despite the tongue lashing they can expect in closed conference session.

Saudi Arabian Oil Minister Ali Naimi, however, whose country is the linchpin of world oil, says he sees no reason for further decline in prices, which are down from $25 per barrel late in 1996 to around $18 now.
"We would like everyone to honour their commitments," he told reporters. But he also said that "demand is good. There is no reason for prices to go lower."
He thought demand could absorb likely OPEC volume. At the highest in 17 years, it was assessed in May by Western monitors at some 27 million barrels daily, two million above an agreed ceiling.
The Saudis argue that the northern winter brings a seasonal upswing in demand and that industry stock cover is below what it was a year ago.
Latest gyrations in a skittish oil futures market seemed to support a sanguine view.
Prices had been rallying on renewed tensions between Iraq and the United Nations.
They soon skidded when the minister of Iraq, Amir Rasheed, said he expected a deal to resume U.N.-supervised oil exports, halted late in May, of up to 750,000 barrels a day within 10 days.
But in the event the London North Sea August crude contract ended only 11 cents down at $17.88 per barrel.
Iran's oil minister, Gholamreza Aghazadeh, however, sounded less relaxed about the cartel quota busting, insisting that "any decision without stopping the violations does not pay".
But delegates said privately that apart from lambasting Venezuela's Erwin Arrieta and other alleged violators, it was hard to see what OPEC could do to police quota discipline.
They said the Saudis seemed in no mood to threaten to turn up their own taps as a retaliatory measure. And the Venezuelans are ready to say that the entire quota system is flawed.
Petroleos de Venezuela, their state oil company, has said that OPEC should abandon quotas altogether and opt for a policy of expanding its share of the world market.
Arrieta, assessed by monitors to be 800,000 barrels above his quota, says he will not actually demand that quotas be abolished, but that he would like to air ideas for change.
